title: Which interventions bring a polarized society back together, and does contact backfire?
summary: 1,000 simulated people in two camps (opinions near 0.2 and 0.8, 95% of ties within camp) follow bounded confidence (Deffuant et al. 2000) with optional repulsion from distant views (Jager & Amblard 2005); the model reproduces Deffuant’s floor(1/(2ε)) cluster count and the Hegselmann–Krause consensus threshold. Six levers are swept over dose, tolerance ε 0.2–0.4 and rejection threshold τ (none, 0.9–0.6), 10 societies each. Rewiring ties across camps never merges them below ε = 0.4 and is the only lever that backfires: at τ = 0.7, rewiring 10% of ties sends everyone to the extremes (10% with no lever). Over 25 settings at top dose, a ladder of committed voices merges the camps in 24, a moderate broadcast or committed moderates in 19, a one-off nudge in 14, raising tolerance in 8 and bridging in 2 (more people at the extremes in 10). A ladder must be spaced for the least tolerant: built for ε = 0.3 when the real one is 0.2, it merges none of 10. Tolerance, rejection threshold and the network are not measured for any real population and are swept, not sourced; opinions are one-dimensional and contact here changes positions only, not prejudice. A follow-up seeds a threshold (complex) contagion on Watts–Strogatz graphs: on clustered networks a patch of 2–3 neighbours starts a cascade that spread-out or random seeds need 12–20 to match, and with threshold 3 nothing past 40 seeds works once ties are rewired (stylised: threshold, degree and graph family chosen, not measured). A third follow-up runs Axelrod’s culture model with a common broadcast: at F = 5, q = 10 on a 20×20 lattice a broadcast heard 30% of the time fragments a society that is one culture without it (largest culture 99% → 26% of sites), because sites sharing no feature with the media never interact with it; the F = 10 order–disorder drop appears at q ≈ 30–50 on small lattices, not reproducing Castellano et al.’s qc ≈ 300 (lattices to L = 150, not run here). A fifth follow-up builds a toy structural-demographic civilization (Turchin 2003): across 864 parameter cells (none measured) it never produces secular cycles, with or without a doubled tax, an elite cap or a welfare transfer, so it cannot yet say which levers damp them. With lags and a collapse reset it does cycle (16 cells with collapses 150–400 years apart), and a paired cell-by-cell test over 576 cells then separates the levers: raising the tax share from 0.3 to 0.45 cuts collapses in 207 of 330 collapsing cells and ends them in 66, lowering it to 0.2 adds collapses in all 179 cells it changes and starts them in 70 quiet ones, while an elite cap cuts them in 15 to 89 cells (tightening from 0.06 to 0.04) and a welfare transfer of 0.4 of rent in 148 while raising population 110%; in this closure collapse is driven by a weak state, not by elite overproduction. A sixth follow-up puts agents on a 7-point scale behind a pluggable policy (a deterministic stub; a real language model plugs in through one environment variable, none is called here): rounding alone leaves the ladder merging 0 of 10 societies (24 of 25 settings continuous), and 20% decision noise merges every society with no lever at all, so any model run needs its own no-lever baseline. A seventh follow-up checks Centola et al.’s 25% tipping point for conventions with a memory-M naming game: the critical committed fraction is set by memory (11% at M = 3, 24–26% at M = 11–13, 42% at 201; groups of 20 within 0.03 of mean field; Xie et al.’s binary-agreement pc = 0.0979 reproduced), and on a ring lattice a clustered patch of committed people never flips the rest while randomly placed ones do from 10%, the reverse of the contagion seeding result (memory and network swept, not measured). Includes an interactive browser simulator.
lede: which interventions bring a polarized society back together? In an opinion-dynamics model with backfire swept from none to strong, bridging ties across camps never merges them and at a rejection threshold of 0.7 rewiring 10% of ties drives everyone to the extremes, while a ladder of committed voices within reach merges them in 24 of 25 settings (moderate broadcast 19, nudge 14, tolerance 8, bridging 2); interactive simulator included (tolerance and backfire are swept, not measured).
